brackets: Apply for up to £60k for projects with less than 5 years to patient benefit, or significant leadership by clinicians, nurses, and allied health professionals (AHPs).

pumpPriming.title: Determining the feasibility and acceptability of Amygdala and Insula retraining (AIR) treatment to alleviate fatigue in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (DAIMoN)
pumpPriming.description:
People with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), including polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis, frequently experience severe fatigue. Fatigue is often the symptom that affects daily life the most, reducing physical activity, social participation, ability to work and overall quality of life. Current approaches such as drug treatments for MPNs do not reliably improve fatigue, meaning there is an unmet need for effective non-pharmacological approaches.

This study will investigate whether an online self-management programme called Amygdala and Insula Retraining (AIR) is acceptable and feasible for people living with MPN-related fatigue. AIR is a brain-retraining programme that combines neuroplasticity techniques, mindfulness practices and lifestyle support. Previous research has suggested that AIR may reduce fatigue in conditions such as fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome and Long COVID. However, it has never been studied in people with MPNs which is needed before a larger study will be done in the future.

Approximately 30 participants with MPNs and significant fatigue will be recruited from East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust. Participants will receive access to the AIR programme for 12 weeks and will complete online questionnaires to measure fatigue and quality of life at study entry (baseline), and 4, 12 and 24 weeks later. Physical activity will also be measured using wrist-worn accelerometers at baseline, 12 and 24 weeks. At the end of the study, a subgroup of participants (around 10) will be interviewed to understand their experiences of using the programme and participating in the research, and learning more about their suggestions for a larger study.

The main aim is to determine whether the intervention and study design are acceptable and practical before undertaking a larger randomised clinical trial. If successful, this research could lead to a low-cost, accessible intervention that improves fatigue and quality of life for people living with MPNs and potentially other blood cancers.

pumpPriming.title: Validating CLIC1 as a viable therapeutic target for the treatment of glioblastoma
pumpPriming.piName: Dr Antony Oliver & Prof Erika Mancini
pumpPriming.institution: Genome Damage and Stability Centre & Sussex Drug Discovery Centre, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
Cancer cells often survive and spread by switching on proteins that healthy cells keep switched off. This project focuses on one such protein, called CLIC1. In healthy cells CLIC1 sits harmlessly inside the cell, but in many cancers it changes shape and moves to the cell's outer membrane, where it appears to help tumours grow, invade and resist treatment. We are studying glioblastoma (an aggressive brain tumour) as a particularly hard-to-treat cancer in which CLIC1 is unusually abundant. People with this type of cancer currently have very few effective treatments and, too often, poor outcomes.

Our idea is to develop a new kind of drug that keeps CLIC1 locked in its harmless internal form, stopping it from moving to the membrane and driving cancer. We have already made the protein in the laboratory and, working with a national research facility, found small molecules that stick to it in exactly the right place. But, before these can be developed into medicines, we must answer some basic but unresolved questions: how, and how much, does CLIC1 move to the cell membrane? In this project we will build a reliable laboratory test to measure this, use it to confirm which part of the protein controls the ‘switch’, and check that our early drug molecules can block it.

Why this matters: if we succeed, we will have shown that blocking CLIC1 is a genuine, measurable way to attack this cancer — the essential first step toward a completely new class of treatment. In the longer term, this could also offer new options to patients with bile duct and pancreatic cancers (which also have high CLIC1 levels), who urgently need them.

pumpPriming.title: Closing the Menopause Care Gap After Breast Cancer: Co-design and Evaluation of an Integrated Specialist Menopause Pathway
pumpPriming.institution: Breast Services, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
pumpPriming.description:
Many women go through an early menopause after breast cancer treatment. Symptoms such as hot flushes, poor sleep, vaginal dryness, low mood, anxiety, tiredness and changes in sexual wellbeing can have a big impact on daily life. For some women, these symptoms can make it difficult to continue important cancer treatments, such as hormone therapy.

Getting the right help can be difficult. Menopause services are not available in the same way everywhere in the NHS, and women may not know where to go for support. Healthcare professionals may also have little experience of managing menopause after cancer treatment.

Our team has already set up a specialist menopause clinic for women with breast cancer. We are listening to patients, evaluating the clinic and carrying out a national survey to understand how menopause care is currently provided across the UK.

What we learn will help us work in partnership with women with breast cancer and healthcare professionals to improve menopause care within Sussex. We first plan to do a survey and interviews with patients who have used the services. Then we will create simple and practical resources together, such as patient information and videos, and clear referral routes, consultation guides and training for healthcare professionals.

We will test these improvements in our specialist clinic for 6 months to see whether they make a real difference to women and can work well as part of routine NHS care. We will also explore how this type of service could support women who have been treated for gynaecological cancers.

Our long-term aim is to develop a leading menopause support service for women affected by cancer. We hope our approach can be shared with other NHS services, helping more women to get the right support and improve their quality of life during and after cancer treatment.

pumpPriming.title: A Systems-Biology Approach Characterising NF-κB Induction of CD70 in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
pumpPriming.institution: Department of Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Brighton and Sussex Medical School
pumpPriming.description:
Diffuse Large B-cell lymphoma is an aggressive and heterogeneous haematological malignancy. Each year in the UK, roughly 5,000 people are diagnosed and the standard of care immunochemotherapy or antibody drug conjugate (ADC) regimes offered as treatments confer a high rate of refractory disease or relapse in 30–40% of patients. Highly targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T therapies have a high rate of failure in this disease, with only limited improvements in progression free survival.

My PhD project focuses on the nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) pathway, which has been extensively studied in its role in promoting tumorigenesis and treatment resistance across many haematological malignancies. In DLBCL, NF-κB is established to be activated by genetic mutations harboured by malignant cells and by components of the DLBCL tumour microenvironment (TME), with higher incidence in poor-prognosis DLBCL subtypes. My project is aided by a computational model that simulates NF-κB signalling and induction of NF-κB target genes. I use this to investigate how heterogeneity in NF-κB subunits (RelA, cRel, RelB) and forms of NF-κB stimulation (canonical/non-canonical) influences the TME via NF-κB-mediated receptor and cytokine expression by DLBCL cells. Single-cell RNA-Seq reveals that TME-derived CD40-ligand (CD40L) and B-cell activating factor (BAFF) activate DLBCL cells, which converge on the non-canonical NF-κB pathway and the RelB subunit.

In the first year of my PhD, I discovered a novel link between the NF-κB subunit RelB and the T-cell co-stimulatory molecule CD70. Elevated expression of CD70 in DLBCL is associated with reduced overall survival and cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell exhaustion in the TME. CD70 is also known to promote the exhaustion of CAR-T cells. This proposal seeks support to purchase the additional consumables required to investigate whether RelB regulates CD70 expression in DLBCL and generate quantitative data for modelling of NF-κB subunit-specific control of the secretomes of heterogeneous DLBCLs. This data will be used to inform parameters in the computational model, allowing more accurate prediction of the DLBCL-TME axis that underscores disease pathology and treatment resistance. Identification of RelB as an inducer of CD70 will open up targeting of the non-canonical NF-κB pathway as an option to mitigate the CAR-T failure seen in DLBCL.

pumpPriming.title: Incorporating Compassion Focused Therapy into the standard of care at a regional Cancer Centre in the UK – A 2-phase feasibility study
pumpPriming.institution: Sussex Cancer Centre, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
pumpPriming.description:
People living with cancer often experience anxiety, low mood, and self-criticism, particularly at stressful times such as scans, clinic appointments, and treatment decisions. These emotional difficulties can affect quality of life and how people cope with treatment. At the same time, cancer staff work in emotionally demanding environments and are at risk of stress and burnout, which can also affect patient care. There is a need for practical, accessible approaches that support emotional wellbeing for both patients and staff within routine cancer services.

Compassion Focused Therapy (CFT) is a psychological approach that helps people develop a kinder and more supportive way of relating to themselves and others. Research shows that CFT can reduce anxiety and depression and improve emotional wellbeing. A simple way of introducing CFT is through the “Three Circles” model, which helps people understand and balance three emotional systems linked to threat, drive, and soothing. This model can be shared using a digital app and group sessions, creating a shared and easy-to-understand language of compassion within a cancer centre.

This study will explore whether introducing the Three Circles model into routine care at a UK cancer centre is practical, acceptable, and helpful. The research will take place in two phases. In the first phase, cancer patients receiving active treatment and frontline cancer staff will be invited to take part in group sessions supported by the app. We will measure changes in anxiety, mood, stress, and wellbeing over time, and compare results with a group who receive the intervention later. In the second phase, the approach will be offered more widely to assess how many people choose to use it and how easily it can be embedded into everyday practice.

If successful, this research could lead to a low-cost and scalable way of improving emotional wellbeing, supporting compassionate care, and enhancing patient and staff experience as part of standard cancer treatment.

pumpPriming.title: Culturally Adapted Cancer Early-Detection Materials: A Community-Led Pilot for Breast and Prostate Cancer within Ethnically Minoritised Communities in Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
This project is a community-led pilot to improve understanding of breast and prostate cancer early detection among ethnically minoritised communities in Sussex. Working with bilingual community members and building on existing, trusted cancer information, we will adapt early-detection and self-checking guidance into culturally sensitive, multilingual formats. These may include short videos, visual guides, and translated explanations shared through community networks. The project will test these materials with participants and gather feedback on clarity, confidence, and emotional response.

Research and local community evidence show that people from ethnically minoritised communities are more likely to experience delays in diagnosis, difficulty understanding screening information, and anxiety when navigating cancer services. Language barriers, cultural stigma, and lack of trusted information contribute to lower screening uptake and later presentation. This project asks whether culturally adapted education, delivered through trusted community routes, can improve understanding, confidence, and willingness to engage with early detection and healthcare services. Answering this question is essential to reducing avoidable inequalities in cancer outcomes.

During this pilot, we expect to engage 50–60 community members directly through workshops, outreach, or small group sessions, with materials reaching an estimated 150–200 people through wider sharing. We aim for at least 60% of participants to report changes to understanding of early signs and screening processes, and at least 70% to report increased confidence to seek help or attend screening. Participants will also be invited to share short reflections on emotional reassurance and reduced anxiety.

The findings will provide practical evidence on how culturally responsive education can support earlier engagement with cancer services. This learning will inform screening programmes, primary care networks, and cancer support services, improving communication and patient experience. Pilot data will also underpin future funding applications to expand this approach across Sussex and beyond.

pumpPriming.title: Cancer Cell Poisoning by targeting PANK4
pumpPriming.institution: School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) are highly aggressive cancers of the brain and blood, respectively. Most people diagnosed with these cancers don’t live beyond the first year, highlighting how urgently we need better, targeted treatments to improve patients’ outcomes.

In a recent study, our laboratory discovered a previously unidentified weakness in GBM called Pantothenate Kinase 4 (PANK4), a little-studied protein long thought to be inactive. We found that PANK4 acts like a drain inside the cell, clearing away harmful substances before they can build up and cause damage. Because cancer cells operate close to their maximum stress levels, blocking PANK4 overwhelms the system, causing toxic accumulation and selective cancer cell poisoning. Exploiting these weaknesses by targeting critical survival safeguards like PANK4 offers an exciting way to treat cancer; however, a better understanding of how PANK4 works is still required.

An independent study at the University of Sussex identified PANK4 as a vulnerability when DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) – a gene often mutated in AML and whose mutations can appear early in pre-leukaemic cells – is defective, making it a critical window for early intervention to stop the disease from developing. Furthermore, collaborators in Sweden recently identified a novel compound targeting PANK4, a protein never before targeted by cancer therapeutics, providing a promising route to drug development.

These complementary findings have brought together a multidisciplinary network of collaborators across the SCRC member institutes and SLU (Sweden). Building on our finding linking PANK4 with GBM resistance, the proposed work offers an exciting opportunity to further elucidate PANK4’s metabolic functions, validate its broader potential as a therapeutic target in AML and assess novel pharmacological inhibitors of PANK4. Ultimately, this proposed study will generate the essential pilot data required for me, as the lead applicant, to pursue a larger independent funding application.

pumpPriming.title: Investigating Wnt-NF-κB crosstalk in aggressive lymphomas to guide targeted therapy
pumpPriming.institution: Department of Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Brighton and Sussex Medical School
pumpPriming.description:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common type of aggressive blood cancer. Standard treatment cures many patients, but around 40% do not respond or relapse. One reason for this is that lymphoma cells can “ignore” signals that should normally cause them to die. These survival signals often come from communication between the cancer cells and their surrounding environment in the body, known as the tumour microenvironment.

This project focuses on two key communication systems inside cancer cells called the Wnt and NF-κB pathways. Both pathways can help cancer cells survive and resist treatment. Recent studies suggest that these pathways may “talk” to each other, creating a powerful survival network that makes lymphoma harder to treat. However, this interaction has never been fully studied in DLBCL.

Our research will first test how Wnt and NF-κB pathways become active in different lymphoma cells, both alone and together. We will then examine how this activity changes the expression of genes that help cancer cells survive, including MYC and MCL1, which are linked to drug resistance. Finally, we will test whether using targeted drugs to block both pathways at the same time can make resistant lymphoma cells sensitive to treatment again. By mapping how these pathways interact, we aim to identify biomarkers that can predict which patients are likely to resist current therapies. In the future, this work could support more personalised treatments for aggressive lymphoma. Patients whose tumours show combined Wnt and NF-κB activity could benefit from therapies that block these survival pathways alongside standard treatments, ultimately improving response rates, survival, and reducing relapse.

pumpPriming.title: A new therapeutic option in acute myeloid leukaemia
pumpPriming.institution: Genome Damage and Stability Centre & Sussex Drug Discovery Centre, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an aggressive and often fatal blood cancer, particularly in older adults. It occurs when immature white blood cells build up in the bone marrow, blocking the production of healthy blood cells. A major challenge in treating AML is the high rate of relapse, especially in patients whose cancer contains a mutation called FLT3-ITD. This genetic change drives rapid cell growth and is linked to poor outcomes and resistance to current treatments.

Researchers at the Sussex Drug Discovery Centre are exploring a new treatment approach for this difficult-to-treat type of AML. Their focus is on a protein called BLM, which helps cancer cells manage the stress of rapid growth. Early studies show that AML cells with the FLT3-ITD mutation are especially vulnerable when BLM is blocked, suggesting they rely heavily on it to survive.

The team has developed a new compound, UOS-BLMi, that inhibits BLM activity. In this project, they will test UOS-BLMi on a broad range of AML cell lines, including those with and without the FLT3-ITD mutation. The goal is to confirm whether FLT3-ITD-positive cells are particularly sensitive to BLM inhibition and to see whether combining UOS-BLMi with existing drugs could help delay or prevent resistance. If results are positive, they will also test UOS-BLMi on healthy blood cells to assess safety.

This research addresses a major unmet need by aiming to develop a targeted therapy for AML patients who currently have few effective options. If successful, it could pave the way for a personalised treatment strategy that improves outcomes while reducing side effects. The findings will provide essential early-stage data to support further drug development, with the long-term aim of delivering a new, more effective treatment to patients.

followOnFunding.title: Innovative Pilot Grant: Developing a new treatment for an aggressive form of AML (co-PI with Prof Erika Mancini)

pumpPriming.title: Developing personalised prognostic models for glioblastoma patients through computational modelling
pumpPriming.institution: University of Sussex & Sussex Cancer Centre, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
pumpPriming.description:
Glioblastoma is the most aggressive type of brain cancer, with about 2,000 people diagnosed each year in the UK. It tends to affect older adults, who are less likely to receive the most intensive treatments. Unfortunately, most of the information available online about how long someone with glioblastoma might live is based on younger and healthier patients who do receive the most aggressive treatments. This means that many patients, especially older or less well patients, do not have access to information that reflects their own situation.

Some online tools are available that try to estimate how long a person might live with glioblastoma, based on their individual details. However, these tools often rely on outdated data, information from large hospitals in other countries, or from clinical trials, and so they do not represent the typical UK patient. Because of this, the estimates they provide may not be very accurate or helpful for most people diagnosed with glioblastoma in the UK.

To change this, we have created a large and up-to-date database of patients from almost every hospital in the UK that treats glioblastoma. We plan to use advanced computer models to better understand why some people live longer than others after being diagnosed. Our aim is to create a tool that gives doctors more accurate and personalised information to share with patients about how long they might live, based on where they are in their treatment.

We also have detailed information on how well different treatments work at different stages. This will help us study how changing treatment approaches could improve survival for people with glioblastoma across the UK. In the long run, we hope this research will help us advocate and push for better care and new studies, especially for patients who are often left out of current research.

pumpPriming.title: Identification of novel DNA2 helicase inhibitors for the treatment of cancer
pumpPriming.institution: Genome Damage and Stability Centre, School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
All cells must faithfully replicate their entire DNA before cell division. This is a particular challenge for cancer cells, which do not follow an orderly replication programme and therefore suffer from what is referred to as “replication stress”. Our recent work shows that the protein DNA2 plays a critical role in the cellular replication stress response. This can explain why highly proliferative cancer cells, and a range of different tumour types, express high levels of DNA2. A dependence of cancer cells on DNA2 may be exploited to kill cancer cells by stress-overload if the protein can be inactivated.

After 30 years of study by many laboratories, our recent findings have enabled us to visualize the actions of DNA2 in cells for the first time. Using this new ability to monitor DNA2 activity, we found that current small-molecule inhibitors intended to target DNA2 in cancer cells are in fact inadequate and ineffective. With a reliable read-out of DNA2 activity now in hand, we therefore propose to translate our fundamental research breakthrough into biomedical application by screening a chemical library for genuine DNA2 inhibitors that can be developed into therapeutic agents.

This work will make a promising new anti-cancer target accessible for clinical use. We anticipate that effective DNA2 inhibitors may deliver broad patient benefits. This is because many different cancer types are characterized by replication stress, making them vulnerable to DNA2 inhibition. For patients with pancreatic cancer, particular advantages may be expected because high DNA2 levels in pancreatic cancer are linked to poor prognosis and effective treatment options for the disease are currently lacking; DNA2 inhibitors may help to close this treatment gap.

pumpPriming.title: A proof-of-concept investigation of a new model to explain fatigue experienced post breast cancer treatment
pumpPriming.institution: School of Education, Sport and Health Sciences, University of Brighton
pumpPriming.description:
Our brain constantly processes information coming from our senses. According to new scientific models, when impaired, these processes lead to feeling fatigued. While people with and beyond cancer are likely to experience fatigue, these models have yet to be tested in cancer patients. We will therefore compare sensory information processing capabilities of cancer patients and healthy participants. We also want to see if our two groups perceive fatigue differently during a physical task and if these differences relate to sensory abilities. Finally, we will draw immune profiles and record other measures such as body composition, physical activity and sleep disturbance, to help explain our findings fully.

We are a newly formed team of oncologist, psychiatrist and researchers from Sussex. This project will enable us to find the best way to collaborate as we ambition to carry out more together. We also have new facilities (Falmer campus, University of Brighton) and want to evaluate how to best do research there with people who live with and beyond cancer.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK (15% of new cancer cases) with a higher prevalence (>50%) of moderate to severe fatigue than for other cancers. So we will study this patient group first. We will recruit patients who have just finished their treatment because fatigue is likely present then and can remain very debilitating after treatment. Patients also told us they are more available to engage at this point in their journey. Cancer-related fatigue is recognized as a significant and distressing symptom and both causes and management strategies are key research priorities in the UK. This project will enable us to study its cause so patients and carers can understand the symptom better, to then move on to developing interventions to help all beat it.

pumpPriming.title: Translational in vivo models for evaluating novel therapies to overcome tumour microenvironment-mediated drug resistance in DLBCL
pumpPriming.institution: Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Brighton and Sussex Medical School
pumpPriming.description:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common type of blood cancer. While standard treatment works for about 60% of patients, 40% either do not respond or experience relapse, highlighting the need for better treatment options. One major reason for treatment failure is that some cancer cells can survive therapy (drug resistance). These surviving tumour cells are often supported by the “normal” cells surrounding the tumour, known as the tumour microenvironment (TME), which help the tumour survive and grow.

Our research focuses on improving treatment for patients who do not respond well to standard therapies. A promising drug target in DLBCL is Bcl-2, a protein which helps cancer cells survive. However, attempts to use venetoclax, a drug which targets this protein, have so far failed in clinical trials. We have found that interactions with cells in the TME cause resistance to venetoclax. However, combining venetoclax with another drug that blocks a protein called NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) reversed this resistance in lab experiments.

The next step toward bringing this combination treatment to patients is to test the drug combination in mouse models of DLBCL which model the human disease better than lab experiments. However, current mouse models do not mimic the TME adequately and thus often lead to drugs that worked in mice being ineffective in humans. Therefore, in this proposal we aim to develop better “humanised” mouse models by creating a human-like immune system in mice and then introducing DLBCL cells. These models will allow us to study the cancer and TME interactions more closely and test our new drug combination effectively.

pumpPriming.title: Increasing physical activity levels in the least active colorectal cancer patients preparing for surgery
pumpPriming.institution: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust & SHORE-C, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
People who undergo colorectal cancer surgery do better if they are physically active. This project is the first step in developing an inclusive intervention to help less active people get active. The next step will be to use the information collected to ‘co-produce’ a user-friendly activity intervention through partnering with patients, the public and health care professionals.

In this first project, we will review previous research exploring what has been done to increase activity in less active cancer patients; interview a diverse group of around 20 patients who have had colorectal cancer surgery to understand their thoughts on what to include in the intervention, how it should be delivered, whether technology (e.g. smartphones) could help, and what a good recovery looks like; and set up a co-production panel of patients, public members and health care professionals.

Colorectal cancer is the fourth most common cancer in the UK. For physical activity, the biggest benefit is moving people from being inactive to doing even light activities. Creating an exercise intervention with patients and public members means it is more likely to be used, supporting patients to be best prepared for surgery so they are more likely to recover well.

pumpPriming.title: PP4 as a novel target in the development of new therapies for ovarian cancer
pumpPriming.institution: Genome Damage and Stability Centre, School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
The DNA in human cells is regularly damaged, even by the body's normal cellular processes. A DNA break in a chromosome can be caused by environmental exposure to radiation and chemicals but may also result from cell metabolism. Left unrepaired or incorrectly repaired, breaks can cause rearrangements of the DNA in our genome, including deletions, translocations and fusions, that have the potential to cause and drive cancer. Fortunately, the body has sophisticated pathways to repair damaged DNA, but these are often altered in cancer to help tumours grow or resist chemotherapy and radiation treatment.

Some cancers suppress the DNA repair system to allow cancer cells to divide with markedly damaged chromosomes. Ovarian cancers make excessive amounts of a protein called PP4, which allows them to ignore DNA repair systems. Blocking or removing PP4 from ovarian cancer cells makes them more susceptible to dying with chemotherapy and can reduce tumour growth. Despite its promise we do not understand, at an atomic level, what PP4 looks like and how it works. Such information is critical for the discovery and development of intelligently designed drugs.

We are aiming to find vulnerabilities in the PP4 protein that we can exploit for drug development. The discovery of new drugs to block PP4 could form the basis for a new class of chemotherapies to treat and cure the disease. Ovarian cancer is lethal, with less than half of women surviving more than 5 years after diagnosis. Resistance to chemotherapy is a problem for ovarian cancers and screening is not beneficial, therefore new therapies are much needed.

followOnFunding.title: Springboard Award — Understanding the molecular mechanisms that terminate DNA damage signalling

pumpPriming.title: Targeting Wnt signalling through a USP axis in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)
pumpPriming.institution: School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex
pumpPriming.description:
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an aggressive type of blood cancer that produces defective immature white blood cells which eventually lead to bone marrow failure. Adults and children can get AML, but typically this disease is diagnosed in older people and has dismal survival rates. Therefore, there is an urgent medical need for alternative targeted treatments with reduced side-effects.

Most AML cases present with overexpression of a cancer-promoting protein called beta-catenin yet there remains no approved effective targeting drug. Beta-catenin promotes leukaemia by interacting with other proteins, so our lab investigated these partner proteins and discovered a family of enzymes called ubiquitin specific proteases (USPs). USPs protect molecules from disposal by removing a ‘label’ called ubiquitin which would otherwise mark the molecule for destruction. This process is very carefully controlled in normal healthy cells to ensure cancer-promoting proteins like beta-catenin are restricted. However, leukaemia cells can hijack this system to boost the level of harmful proteins such as beta-catenin and promote AML development.

This project will exploit the expertise of multiple institutes within the Sussex Cancer Research Centre to discover the overall level of specific USPs in leukaemia patient samples, their contribution to healthy blood and AML development, and how they regulate the beta-catenin molecule. Acquiring this initial information will allow us to design a new class of drugs that are safe and effective at reducing the levels of beta-catenin in blood cells through targeting its USP partners. Successful completion of this pilot study will provide a junior cancer researcher with the necessary resources to prepare their first research funding bid.

creativeEngagement.title: 'Pharmakon' and 'Calle Incurabili (The Narrow Path of Cure)'
creativeEngagement.description: This project has two parts, one located at the Falmer campus, and one found across the SCRC campus. These artworks arose from Markus’s physical and psychological experiences during and after treatment for an incurable blood cancer.

creativeEngagement.title: 'Words from the Waiting Room'
creativeEngagement.description:
This project offers an innovative way to put people with lived experience at the heart of our research.

Through creative workshops, people with lived experience of cancer will explore their own stories, using facilitated creative writing and collage. Co-production of artistic pieces containing words and collage will create the opportunity for the patient voice to be heard. By using the experience of the waiting room, where people often ruminate on their disease and consultation, this project will give unique insights into the lived experience of those served by our research.

studentships.title: AI solutions to guide treatment strategies for Cancers of Unknown Primaries (CUPs)
studentships.institution: School of Life Sciences, University of Sussex & University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
studentships.description:
In general, the types of treatment available to a cancer patient are determined by the type or ‘site’ of the original tumour. However, for 3–5% of all cancers, termed ‘cancer of unknown primary’ or ‘CUPs’, the original tumour site is unknown, making it particularly challenging to decide on the best treatment strategy for the disease as it presents at diagnosis in secondary sites. For a minority of CUP patients (15–20%), the tumour can be attributed to a distinct clinical entity that benefits from primary site-specific treatment; however, the remaining 80–85% of patients belong to a group with a poor CUP prognosis. In Sussex, despite extensive clinical and diagnostic work-up, including physical examination, radiological imaging, and histopathological investigation, approximately 300–500 of the cancers diagnosed annually are designated as CUPs.

The major aim of this project is the development of artificial intelligence (AI) methods to aid diagnosis and inform treatment strategies to improve outcomes for Sussex CUP patients. This project is a collaboration between the Pearl Bioinformatics Laboratory at the University of Sussex and the CUP Multi-Disciplinary Team at the Royal Sussex County Hospital, University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, supported by both the University of Sussex and Brighton and Sussex Medical School.

followOnFunding.title: Strategy for the findability and accessibility of CRUK data

studentships.title: Targeting NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) for the treatment of multiple myeloma
studentships.description:
Multiple myeloma (MM) is a devastating blood cancer that remains largely incurable despite the introduction of a range of new treatment options. The NF-κB pathway plays a critical role in MM progression, and NF-κB-inducing kinase (NIK) has emerged as a key regulator of tumour cell survival, immune evasion, and drug resistance.

This PhD studentship, supported by Dr William Priddy, Brighton and Sussex Medical School, and the Sussex Cancer Fund, explores how NIK contributes to multiple myeloma and evaluates novel strategies to target it for therapeutic benefit. Using CRISPR/shRNA gene manipulation and pharmacological inhibitors in cell lines and patient-derived organoid models, the project investigates how NIK inhibition affects myeloma cell survival, the tumour microenvironment, immune responses, and sensitivity to standard treatments.

studentships.title: Identifying patients most at risk of developing cancer related fatigue
studentships.institution: SHORE-C, Brighton and Sussex Medical School & University of Sussex
studentships.description:
Cancer related fatigue (CRF) is common (estimated prevalence 40–71%) but remains poorly understood and undertreated. In some cases, CRF persists many years after treatment has been completed. Causes of CRF include the cancer itself, related signs and symptoms like anaemia and pain, cancer treatments, comorbidities, and psychological factors, with inflammation most often cited as a major driver.

The purpose of this project is to improve our understanding of CRF by combining patient-reported outcomes and proteomic analysis to test whether it is possible to predict at diagnosis who will go on to experience clinically significant CRF during and after treatment. Through secondary analysis of the HORIZONS cohort alongside a longitudinal study of lung and breast cancer patients at University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, this studentship aims to enable earlier, targeted interventions and identify novel treatment targets.
